clue.text: Old payment of course skimmed off?

indicators.note: Skimming lifts whatever is floating on top, and the top of a down entry is the letter it starts on.

blocks.note: Ascot is the Berkshire racecourse of the royal meeting, offered here as one course among many

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'of course' as the throwaway aside and there is nothing to work on; read it as 'of a course' and a famous racecourse is standing there waiting to be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Old payment → SCOT: scot was a medieval household tax, a word that survives now only in 'scot-free', meaning let off without paying.

clue.text: Gauls reportedly in French city?

definitions.note: The final S belongs to a proper name, not to a plural: the city is one place, and the S the wordplay supplies is a verb ending instead.

indicators.note: What is reported is passed on by mouth, so the first word is to be heard rather than read letter by letter.

blocks.note: the ancient French people said aloud are galls, and to gall somebody is to make them cross

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to picture Gauls wandering round a French town, which is exactly the wrong place to look: the Frenchness is in the definition, and the Gauls are only a sound.
explanation.definitionFit: French city → ANGERS: the old capital of Anjou, on the Maine in western France, is one of the country's cathedral cities.

clue.text: Booming ace in tennis, or tennis’s first shot

indicators.note: A thing described as shot has been wrecked beyond its old shape, and letters wrecked that way come back in another order.
It picks out where a word begins, asking for one letter off the front rather than the whole name.

blocks.note: the ace of a suit is written A at the card table, a standard single-letter sense
anagram fodder, eight letters, comma and all
the letter the word tennis opens with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ace in tennis' wants to be a service winner and 'first shot' wants to be the serve. Both are material and instruction instead, which is why the clue reads so smoothly.
explanation.definitionFit: Booming → STENTORIAN: both describe a voice of enormous carrying power, the adjective coming from Stentor, the herald in Homer who shouted like fifty men.

clue.text: See 26 Across
Bomber, a girl I sent up ending in atrocity

indicators.note: Sending something up a down entry pushes it back towards the top, so those letters are read the other way about.
It points at the finish of the word that follows and asks for the single letter sitting there.

blocks.note: taken as it stands
gal is the informal spelling of a girl
the Roman numeral I is one, written out as a word here
the last letter of atrocitY

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a man teasing a girl, and 'atrocity' is the one word that does not fit it — the giveaway that something much darker is being named.
explanation.definitionFit: Bomber → ENOLA GAY: the B-29 that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima, named by its pilot after his mother, so one particular bomber stands for the class.

clue.text: No-win situation The Guardian’s responsibility to turn around?

indicators.note: Turning a thing around presents its far end first, so the letters are taken in the opposite order.

blocks.note: a guardian is the person legally responsible for a ward

explanation.walkthrough: 'No-win situation' is normally an idiom for a hopeless predicament; here it is meant literally, as a result in which nobody wins. The newspaper is a joke on the setter's own paper.
explanation.definitionFit: No-win situation → DRAW: a drawn match ends level, with neither side taking the win, which is the sporting result the phrase describes literally.

clue.text: One crossing the line in entering shipping forecast area

indicators.note: To enter something is to go inside it, so the little word before it lands within the longer one rather than beside it.

blocks.note: Fisher is one of the sea areas read out on the BBC's Shipping Forecast, off the Danish coast
the word itself, used as two letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like grammar holding the sentence up and is the piece being inserted, which is the whole disguise. Every other word points at athletics or the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: One crossing the line → FINISHER: in a race the line is the finish, so whoever reaches it has completed the course rather than dropped out.

clue.text: Rectify state of mind guzzling a barrel of beer

indicators.note: A guzzler takes drink down inside, so the state of mind swallows the other piece whole.

blocks.note: your mood is the state of mind you happen to be in
beer comes in a keg, and the A in front is taken as it stands

explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs on into 25 down. Everything in the clue after the first word is a drinker's evening, and none of it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rectify → MAKE GOOD: to make good a loss, a promise or a damaged wall is to put right what went wrong, the phrase builders and lawyers both use.

clue.text: Study air pressure

blocks.note: to con a text is to study it closely, an old sense crosswords keep alive
an air is a tune, and so is a strain — both mean a melody

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, three separate jobs, and the surface makes them one phrase from a weather forecast. Short clues like this hide the joins by having no joins at all.
explanation.definitionFit: pressure → CONSTRAIN: to pressure someone into acting is to constrain them; the definition is the verb, not the noun the meteorological surface suggests.

clue.text: Educated character fed a refreshing side dish

indicators.note: Something fed to a person goes inside them, so the letter that follows is put within the name.

blocks.note: Rita is the hairdresser taking an Open University course in Willy Russell's play Educating Rita
taken as it stands

explanation.walkthrough: 'Character' is the pointer: it says a name is wanted, and the title of the play supplies one that has been educated.
explanation.definitionFit: refreshing side dish → RAITA: the cool yoghurt-and-cucumber dip served beside a curry precisely to take the heat out of it.

clue.text: Link that is apparently like spam?

indicators.note: It means as far as appearances go, so only the outside is being described and something else is sitting within it.

blocks.note: Spam is the tinned meat, so what resembles it comes in a tin
i.e. is the everyday short form of the Latin id est, that is

explanation.walkthrough: Spam pulls you straight to junk email, which is where the meat's name ended up. The clue wants the tin the meat came in.
explanation.definitionFit: Link → TIE-IN: a tie-in is the commercial connection between, say, a film and the toys sold alongside it, and by extension any link between two things.

clue.text: Pure flower with foul fragrance, ultimately

indicators.note: Something foul has gone rotten, and rotten letters no longer hold the shape they were handed to you in.
At the very end — it asks for the letter the word finishes on and nothing before it.

blocks.note: the flower named is a lily, handed over whole
four letters of raw material, not the joinery the word pretends to be
the last letter of fragrancE

explanation.walkthrough: 'With' reads as grammar and is fodder; 'foul' reads as part of the smell and is the instruction. That double disguise is what makes a short anagram hard.
explanation.definitionFit: Pure → LILY-WHITE: spotless by comparison with the flower, and used of a reputation with nothing whatever to reproach in it.

clue.text: Capital in Paris is at the end of the day in France – go there?

definitions.note: The setter names the place by the errand that takes you to it rather than by a synonym, so the words could not be swapped for the answer in a sentence.

indicators.note: Here it means the upper-case letter a proper name is written with, not a seat of government.

blocks.note: Paris starts with a capital letter, and that single letter is all the wordplay wants
the word taken as it stands

blocks.clueFragment: at the end of the day in France
blocks.note: soir is the French for evening, the end of the day over there

explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital in Paris' invites you to think of France's capital city and asks only for the letter P. The euphemism in the definition is doing the same trick in English.
explanation.definitionFit: go there? → PISSOIR: a pissoir is the French street urinal, so the place is defined by what people go there to do.

clue.text: Average outside cold, with coat off – freezing!

indicators.note: The average is placed outside the other piece, so its letters open and close the answer with the rest between them.
A coat is the layer worn on the outside, so taking it off strips the letters at each end of the word.

blocks.note: par is the normal or average standard, as in up to par
COLD wearing nothing on the outside loses the letter at each end

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the last word look like an exclamation about the weather in the story, and it is the definition standing on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: freezing → POLAR: the poles are the coldest ground on earth, so anything polar is bitterly cold — the word carries the temperature, not just the geography.

clue.text: Tooth that’s new in cutter?

indicators.note: The insertion word: what precedes it goes inside the thing named next, rather than in front of it.

blocks.note: something that gashes is a cutter, the -er turning the verb into the thing that does it
n = new, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutter' looks like a boat or a trade and is an invented agent noun. Gnasher is also the Beano dog, which is why the clue can afford the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Tooth → GNASHER: gnashers is the familiar British word for teeth, from gnashing them, so a single one of them is a gnasher.

clue.text: Lethal whipped cream – take care!

indicators.note: Cream is whipped until it no longer holds the shape it had, and the letters in front are treated the same way.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, rearranged into the two short words at the front
the cream of anything is the best of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Whipped cream' is one thing on the surface and two jobs underneath: only the first word is shuffled, and the cream is the pick of the crop.
explanation.definitionFit: take care! → ALL THE BEST: both are said on parting, wishing somebody well, so the whole phrase answers a whole phrase rather than a word.

clue.text: Mode of ode, say?

blocks.note: the surface reading: a manner or fashion belonging to an ode, the way the poem is put together
the for-example marker — the first word is being offered as an instance, and what it is an instance of is its relation to the second

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here to take apart. The two words are doing it to each other: say 'mode' and 'ode' aloud and the answer is what one is to the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Mode of ode, say? → RHYME: 'mode' chimes with 'ode', so the clue holds up one word as an example of what it is to another.

clue.text: See 28
Big man, as dancing, doing just that?

indicators.note: A dancer never stands still, so the letters in front of the word will not stay in the places they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pointer rather than a word: 'just that' means whatever was said a moment earlier, and what was said a moment earlier is the shuffling instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: doing just that? → SAMBAING: the definition points back at 'dancing', and the answer is performing one particular Brazilian dance.

clue.text: Bird with 14 mentioning celebrated baker?

indicators.note: To mention a thing is to say it out loud, so what follows is heard rather than spelled.

blocks.note: the answer to 14 across is borrowed for its sound, and the G it opens with is silent
Jane Asher is the British actress whose celebration-cake business made her a household name for baking; say this entry and then 14 across and you have said her name

explanation.walkthrough: Two of the puzzle's own answers spoken one after the other make a real person's name, so 14 is borrowed for its sound and never for its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bird → JAY: the jay is the pinkish woodland crow with a flash of blue on the wing, one bird standing in for the general word.

clue.text: Marine’s carried through in cheerful manner

indicators.note: Whatever carries a thing has it aboard, inside itself, so one piece here holds the other within it.

blocks.note: a jolly is Royal Navy slang for a Royal Marine
going through a place is going via it

explanation.walkthrough: Jove is Jupiter, and astrologers held that anyone born under his planet turned out merry — which is where the cheerfulness in the answer comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: in cheerful manner → JOVIALLY: to do something jovially is to do it heartily and in good humour, the adverb formed from jovial.

clue.text: Author Lee articulated – something like that?

indicators.note: To articulate is to pronounce clearly, so the name is to be heard — and the same word is what British roads call a hinged truck.

blocks.note: Laurie Lee wrote Cider with Rosie, and his first name said aloud is spelled quite differently

explanation.walkthrough: One word does both jobs: it tells you to hear the author's first name, and it is the adjective the vague definition is quietly pointing at.
explanation.definitionFit: something like that? → LORRY: the definition points back at 'articulated', and an articulated lorry is the British name for a hinged truck.

clue.text: House where fellow in groovy clothing undressed

indicators.note: Clothes go round whatever is inside them, so this word wraps one piece about the other.
Undressed means stripped of what is worn outside, so the word loses the letter at its front and the letter at its back.

blocks.note: GROOVY with the letter at each end taken off
a fellow is a man

explanation.walkthrough: 'House where fellow' reads like a place with a lodger in it. The house wanted is a dynasty, the sense in which we speak of the House of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: House → ROMANOV: a royal house is a dynasty, and the Romanovs ruled Russia for three centuries until 1917, so one dynasty defines the word by example.

clue.text: Pop is attending church: he had relapsed earlier

indicators.note: To attend somebody is to go along beside them, so these two letters stand next to the church rather than inside it.
A relapse is a slipping back, so those letters arrive in the reverse of the order the clue gives them.
It fixes the order: that piece belongs at the front of the answer, not where its words sit in the sentence.

blocks.note: HE'D is 'he had' shortened, and it has slipped back the other way round
the word taken as it stands
CE is the Church of England, the church a crossword usually means

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes the second half sound like gossip about a man at the service. Dehiscence is the botanist's word for a seed pod splitting along its seam.
explanation.definitionFit: Pop → DEHISCE: a ripe pod dehisces when it bursts open along a line of weakness, which is exactly what popping open means in botany.

clue.text: Reject is blocking sink

indicators.note: Something blocking sits in the way of what it blocks, and this small word sits in the middle of the longer one, splitting it.

blocks.note: to sink is to go down
the word itself, dropped in whole

explanation.walkthrough: Three short words reading like a note left for the plumber, with a separate job hidden in each of them. Short clues rarely mean short work.
explanation.definitionFit: Reject → DISOWN: to disown a person is to refuse to acknowledge them as your own, the flattest and strongest form of rejecting one.

clue.text: One is doddery, right?

indicators.note: Doddery means shaky on the feet, and letters that cannot stand steady will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
r = right, as in a stage direction or a map reference

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: read straight, the sentence describes the person; read again, the same words are the recipe. 'Right?' is both the question tag and a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines: a senior is an elderly person, exactly the one the sentence is describing, with the tag question doing duty as wordplay.

clue.text: Amusing language in which the following might sound like laughter?

blocks.note: read as English it is a pointer, meaning whatever comes next; the setter wants it read as a phrase waiting to be translated, 'the' and 'after'
translate only the first half and leave the second in English, the way the answer does: l'after, said aloud, is laughter

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing to take apart, and no letters to collect. Do to 'the following' what the answer is named for: turn half of it French, leave half English, and you get l'after — which spoken aloud is laughter. The clue is a specimen of the language it defines, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusing language → FRANGLAIS: French and English run together in one sentence for comic effect, and the clue itself is a sample of the mixture.

clue.text: Musical combination of two notes

indicators.note: A combination is what you get by putting things together, so the two pieces are simply laid end to end.

blocks.note: fah is the fourth degree of the sol-fa scale, written as two letters
me is the third degree of that scale in the British spelling of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective and is a noun — the name of a show. The sol-fa scale is where setters go whenever they want short notes: doh, ray, me, fah, soh.
explanation.definitionFit: Musical → FAME: the 1980 film about a New York performing-arts school was turned into a long-running stage musical of the same name.

clue.text: See 8
House visitor for whom knock at the door comes after 4?

definitions.text: for whom knock at the door comes after 4?

blocks.note: 'House!' is the shout that claims a win in a British bingo hall
somebody who calls at your door is a visitor

explanation.walkthrough: Two words of wordplay and the rest of the sentence is the definition, describing the person at the microphone by one line of patter.
explanation.definitionFit: In British bingo every number has its rhyme, and 'knock at the door' is the one for four, so the phrase follows the number when it is called.

clue.text: Curse of Portillo, a Thatcherite

indicators.note: All the concealment signal there is: a part taken out of what comes next, which is about as quiet as a hiding place gets.

blocks.note: four letters running straight on from the end of the surname into the words that follow it

explanation.walkthrough: Michael Portillo was a Conservative cabinet minister under Margaret Thatcher, so the sentence reads as ordinary political comment — and the letters sit inside it in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Curse → OATH: an oath is a profanity as well as a solemn promise, and it is the swearing sense the definition asks for.

clue.text: Imported into Vietnam, Angola’s simple fruit drink

indicators.note: Something imported has been brought in from outside and is now sitting inside, which is where the letters wanted are.

blocks.note: ten consecutive letters, beginning inside the first country and ending inside the last word

explanation.walkthrough: Two countries side by side make a good hiding place, and the run crosses a comma, an apostrophe and two word breaks without a single letter moving.
explanation.definitionFit: fruit drink → MANGO LASSI: a lassi is the Indian yoghurt drink, and the mango version blends the fruit into it, drunk cold alongside a curry.

clue.text: Central European fliers circling on the occidental side of English port

indicators.note: A thing circling goes right round what it circles, so the airline's letters close about the rest.

blocks.note: LOT is the national airline of Poland, a country in central Europe
the occident is the west, so this is the plain phrase 'west of' spelled out

explanation.walkthrough: 'On the occidental side of English' looks like an instruction to take the western half of a word, and it is six letters written out longhand.
explanation.definitionFit: English port → LOWESTOFT: the Suffolk fishing town on the North Sea, the most easterly point in Britain, has been a working harbour for centuries.
